slice: Use Spark Decimal ROUND result types with the existing DataFusion kernel

scope.production_change: Local planner factory reuses constant evaluation and Sail rounding type rules; a small native UDF adapter delegates execution and sorting properties to RoundFunc. Precision is capped before narrowing to u8 in the shared helper.
scope.scale_scope: Decimal128 with an integer constant representable as i32, or NULL. Other coercions and non-Decimal behavior remain incomplete.

provenance.upstream_observation: Inspected Sail main still registers generic DataFusion ROUND. The installed datafusion-spark 54.1.0 ROUND retains the input type, so it does not supply this result-type fix.

corpus.origin: Locally designed precision/scale and constant-expression matrix, guided by Spark RoundBase and the original composed ROUND mismatch; not an upstream CI list.

performance.allocator_method: Wide ROUND only: four balanced timing processes and two execution-counter processes per variant and ANSI mode, for each of default isolated calls, fixed mmap threshold, and fixed mmap plus trim thresholds. Same copied binaries, CPU 2 and every-row checks. Environment overrides apply only to these diagnostic child processes.

limitations: Six original and twenty new value/type or error-stage differences remain. One additional same-stage agreement has a different error cause. These observations do not establish full Spark compatibility.

Numeric comparison checks ordered values, numeric types and error stage. Focused checks add 21 ROUND error causes and preserve 70 earlier error/negative-zero checks. Delta comparison separately checks schema dimensions.
Implicit scale/value coercions, non-Decimal ROUND behavior, extreme negative-scale runtime errors and NULL evaluation order remain separate work.

The 26 existing benchmark controls retain identical rendered physical plans. ROUND retains the same plan structure and kernel but changes the UDF result type; equal rendered text does not mean identical UDF implementations.

Default wide-ROUND timings have large modes and high page-fault counts. Fixed allocator thresholds greatly reduce faults and timing differences, supporting allocator sensitivity but not proving no regression for arbitrary default-allocator workloads. No production allocator setting is changed.
CPU frequency is not fixed and the host is not isolated. Small timing/counter changes do not prove zero overhead or erase earlier planning costs.
